walkthroughs.body_html:
Qualitative Research Methods (HL Extension) — a core area of Psychology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Qualitative Research Methods (HL Extension) brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Qualitative Research Methods (HL Extension).

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Braun and Clarke's 2006 thematic analysis has how many phases?
Reflecting on how the researcher shapes the data is called:
options: Triangulation
Reflexivity
Coding
Saturation

mcqs.q: Why does the cognitive approach use INFERENCE?
options: Because brain scans are unreliable.
Because cognitive psychologists guess instead of measuring.
Mental processes cannot be directly observed, so they are inferred from behaviour.
No relationship.

mcqs.q: According to Maslow, when can self-actualisation be achieved?
options: Only through religious experience.
No relationship.
Anyone can self-actualise at any time through willpower.
Only after lower deficiency needs are largely met.

mcqs.q: What does a correlation of -0.8 indicate?
options: Only through religious experience.
No relationship.
A strong negative relationship.
A weak relationship (because it is negative).

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Naturalistic observation”?
options: In-depth investigation of one individual, group or event; e.g. HM (Milner 1957) on memory.
Recording behaviour in its natural setting without manipulation; high ecological validity, low control.
Braun and Clarke (2006) six-phase method: familiarisation, coding, themes, review, define, write-up.
Researcher reflecting on how their identity and assumptions shape data collection and interpretation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Reflexivity”?
options: In-depth investigation of one individual, group or event; e.g. HM (Milner 1957) on memory.
Guided by a topic list; allows flexibility for follow-up while maintaining comparability across participants.
Braun and Clarke (2006) six-phase method: familiarisation, coding, themes, review, define, write-up.
Researcher reflecting on how their identity and assumptions shape data collection and interpretation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Thematic analysis”?
options: In-depth investigation of one individual, group or event; e.g. HM (Milner 1957) on memory.
Braun and Clarke (2006) six-phase method: familiarisation, coding, themes, review, define, write-up.
Group interview of 6-10 participants; uses interaction to generate data; risk of dominant voices skewing discussion.
Guided by a topic list; allows flexibility for follow-up while maintaining comparability across participants.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Focus group”?
options: Guided by a topic list; allows flexibility for follow-up while maintaining comparability across participants.
Recording behaviour in its natural setting without manipulation; high ecological validity, low control.
Group interview of 6-10 participants; uses interaction to generate data; risk of dominant voices skewing discussion.
Researcher reflecting on how their identity and assumptions shape data collection and interpretation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Case study”?
options: Guided by a topic list; allows flexibility for follow-up while maintaining comparability across participants.
Braun and Clarke (2006) six-phase method: familiarisation, coding, themes, review, define, write-up.
Researcher reflecting on how their identity and assumptions shape data collection and interpretation.
In-depth investigation of one individual, group or event; e.g. HM (Milner 1957) on memory.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Semi-structured interview”?
options: Braun and Clarke (2006) six-phase method: familiarisation, coding, themes, review, define, write-up.
Researcher reflecting on how their identity and assumptions shape data collection and interpretation.
In-depth investigation of one individual, group or event; e.g. HM (Milner 1957) on memory.
